metadata.title: Collaboration and socio-economic inequality: Estimating the effects of intra-school and inter-school inequality on collaborative problem-solving skills

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 microdata for 15-year-olds who took the CPS human-agent assessment, nested within schools and countries. The analytic sample is restricted to respondents with non-missing data; additionally, unanswered CPS and science items are scored as incorrect rather than treated as missing. The manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or any replicate-weight procedure, and the analysis is conducted using a multilevel (HLM) framework rather than ML algorithms that would typically require explicit weight handling. For replication with PISA Data, analysts should apply the appropriate PISA student/sampling weights (and replicate weights if variance estimation is required) to account for the complex survey design and clustering; however, this paper’s weighting strategy is not documented.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable (CPS) is constructed as a proportion of correct answers to the PISA 2015 CPS items rather than using PV-based achievement scores, so plausible values are not applicable. Missing data handling is described as excluding respondents with missing data, and the paper also clarifies that unanswered CPS and science items are scored as incorrect rather than missing. Therefore, PV imputation and PV-related missingness strategies are not part of the analysis pipeline.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses PISA 2015 CPS assessment data for 15-year-olds and limits the analysis to 46 countries that administered the CPS module (not all 72 PISA participants in 2015 applied CPS). The analytic sample includes 102,219 students from 12,510 schools across these 46 countries. Respondents with missing data are excluded (listwise deletion), and the paper specifies that unanswered questions in the CPS and science exams are scored as incorrect rather than treated as missing. For reading and mathematics, the sample is split evenly (50% completing one or the other), but the CPS outcome and the SCIENCE control are used in the reported models; SCIENCE is available for all students in all countries.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Hierarchical linear models (HLM) with randomized intercepts/slopes; unstandardized coefficients (b) and standard errors (s.e.) reported. Intra-school inequality: M1 b=-10.61 (s.e.=1.41, p<0.001); M2 b=-15.02 (s.e.=5.56, p=0.007); M3 b=-4.93 (s.e.=0.65, p<0.001); M4 b=-7.16 (s.e.=2.55, p=0.005). Science control (SCIENCE): M3 b=53.67 (s.e.=0.90, p<0.001); M4 b=53.65 (s.e.=0.88, p<0.001). Inter-school inequality: M1 b=-10.39 (s.e.=4.84, p=0.038); M2 b=-9.89 (s.e.=4.78, p=0.045); M3 b=-1.36 (s.e.=2.82, p=0.632); M4 b=-1.12 (s.e.=2.83, p=0.693).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Grade 10-15 (15-year-olds) Collaborative Problem Solving (CPS) the study leveraged Intra-school SES inequality, ESCS index, and Science achievement (SCIENCE) (plus Family wealth and Generalized trust in extended models) to predict the CPS index, finding that higher intra-school SES inequality is consistently associated with lower CPS performance (e.g., b=-10.61 to b=-7.16 across models) while the inter-school inequality effect disappears once SCIENCE is included. This indicates that reducing within-school socioeconomic stratification and improving students’ academic readiness (as reflected in science performance) may be key levers for strengthening collaborative problem-solving skills, though the study is correlational and uses multilevel modeling rather than causal identification.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2015 CPS performance for 15-year-olds in 46 countries (102,219 students across 12,510 schools), using a multilevel (HLM) framework to estimate how socioeconomic inequality at different levels relates to collaborative problem solving. CPS is operationalized as the proportion of correct answers to the PISA 2015 CPS human-agent items, and the authors exclude respondents with missing data; unanswered CPS and science items are scored as incorrect. Across four HLM specifications, intra-school SES inequality shows a negative and statistically significant association with CPS (b=-10.61 in M1; b=-15.02 in M2; remaining negative in M3 and M4 even after adding SCIENCE). Inter-school inequality is negative in models without SCIENCE but loses statistical significance once SCIENCE is included. The paper also reports small positive associations for generalized trust and moderation patterns with political equality, but it does not use ML algorithms or PV-based achievement scaling.
